fetched_contents.text: Operationalization of Sign Language Phonological Similarity and its Effects on Lexical Access Abstract Cognitive mechanisms for sign language lexical access are fairly unknown. This study investigated whether phonological similarity facilitates lexical retrieval in sign languages using measures from a new lexical database for American Sign Language. Additionally, it aimed to determine which similarity metric best fits the present data in order to inform theories of how phonological similarity is constructed within the lexicon and to aid in the operationalization of phonological similarity in sign language. Sign repetition latencies and accuracy were obtained when native signers were asked to reproduce a sign displayed on a computer screen. Results indicated that, as predicted, phonological similarity facilitated repetition latencies and accuracy as long as there were no strict constraints on the type of sublexical features that overlapped. The data converged to suggest that one similarity measure, MaxD, defined as the overlap of any 4 sublexical features, likely best represents mechanisms of phonological similarity in the mental lexicon. Together, these data suggest that lexical access in sign language is facilitated by phonologically similar lexical representations in memory and the optimal operationalization is defined as liberal constraints on overlap of 4 out of 5 sublexical features—similar to the majority of extant definitions in the literature. ---------------------------------------- Decades of research have been dedicated to understanding how humans retrieve lexical information. Psycholinguistic theories of lexical access have hypothesized that words are activated by both top-down semantic and bottom-up phonological coactivation (Harley, 1993; Levelt, 1993). As such, during lexical access of a target word, similar-sounding words can be coactivated, modulating retrieval latencies. However, most theories of lexical access are restricted to spoken language research. Few studies have attempted to characterize lexical access in sign language (for a review see Corina & Knapp, 2006a). One reason for the paucity of studies has been a lack of quantitative lexical information (e.g., frequency, neighborhood density) for sign languages. With the emergence of several new lexical databases for sign languages (e.g., Fenlon et al., 2014; Gutierrez-Sigut, Costello, Baus, & Carreiras, 2016; Johnston, 2001) new studies can now be constructed to empirically investigate the role of lexical properties on sign access. As such, the present study aimed to characterize the role of phonological similarity on sign language repetition using neighborhood density metrics from ASL-LEX (Caselli, Sevcikova-Sehyr, Cohen-Goldberg, & Emmorey, 2017), a new large-scale lexical database for American Sign Language (ASL). A second aim of this study was to attempt to identify a neighborhood density metric that is both theoretically and empirically motivated. ASL-LEX provides three different neighborhood density metrics, which differ on the type of phonological similarity, and it is unclear which would be most appropriate for studies on sign access. Together, this manuscript attempts to clarify the role of phonological similarity in lexical access by comparing the results herein to those of previous studies and taking a principled approach to select a robust measure of phonological similarity in signed languages. Literature Review Lexical access is dependent on a number of properties, one of which is phonological similarity of a target item to other lexical items. The structure of sign language phonology may influence both the structure of the lexicon as well as the psycholinguistic mechanisms used for lexical access. Despite sign languages being natural languages with all of the same linguistic characteristics of spoken language (for a review see Emmorey, 2002; Sandler & Lillo-Martin, 2006), spoken and sign languages diverge greatly in how phonological information is represented and articulated on the body, which impacts the nature of the linguistic signal. Spoken languages rely on an auditory-oral input–output signal,1 whereas sign languages take advantage of a visual-manual signal.2 Despite these modality differences, emerging evidence suggests that the psycholinguistic mechanisms for lexical retrieval, recognition, and production are similar (Carreiras, 2010; Corina & Knapp, 2006b; Emmorey & Corina, 1990; Giezen & Emmorey, 2015; MacSweeney, Capek, Campbell, & Woll, 2008; Sandler & Lillo-Martin, 2006; Williams & Newman, 2015, 2016a, c). However, due to various definitions of phonological similarity used in previous studies, it is not clear to what extent different degrees of phonological overlap might affect sign access. Signs are composed of sublexical phonological features, which combine in various ways and can be represented as parameters, similar to spoken words and their sublexical phonological features (Brentari, 1998; Liddell & Johnson, 1989; Sandler, 1989). These sublexical phonological features are contrastive in sign languages insofar as two signs can differ along any number of features. For example, the minimal pair summer3 and ugly in ASL share handshape and movement sublexical features, but differ based on location features. As such, a pair of signs can be judged to be phonologically similar based on their shared parameters, analogous to how pat and bat are phonologically similar words in English. Published in final edited form as: Biling (Camb Engl). 2020 Jan 31;23(5):1032–1044. doi: 10.1017/S1366728919000889 Abstract This study used ERPs to a) assess the neural correlates of cross-linguistic, cross-modal translation priming in hearing beginning learners of American Sign Language (ASL) and deaf highly proficient signers and b) examine whether sign iconicity modulates these priming effects. Hearing learners exhibited translation priming for ASL signs preceded by English words (greater negativity for unrelated than translation primes) later in the ERP waveform than deaf signers and exhibited earlier and greater priming for iconic than non-iconic signs. Iconicity did not modulate translation priming effects either behaviorally or in the ERPs for deaf signers (except in a 800–1000 ms time window). Because deaf signers showed early translation priming effects (beginning at 400ms-600ms), we suggest that iconicity did not facilitate lexical access, but deaf signers may have recognized sign iconicity later in processing. Overall, the results indicate that iconicity speeds lexical access for L2 sign language learners, but not for proficient signers. Keywords: translation recognition, sign language, iconicity, language learning Introduction The human brain can transform arbitrary symbols such as words into meaningful concepts within milliseconds and, even more incredibly, we can learn new vocabulary by making new connections between these arbitrary symbols and their meanings throughout our lives. One goal of research focused on second language (L2) acquisition and processing in adults has been to shed light on how new words are learned as well as how new language systems are built and stored. Several investigators have used the temporal precision of event-related potentials (ERPs) to measure the adult brain’s response to L2 words in proficient bilinguals and learners who have not yet attained L2 proficiency (e.g., Alvarez, Holcomb & Grainger, 2003; Hoshino, Midgley, Holcomb & Grainger, 2010; McLaughlin, Osterhout & Kim, 2004; Midgley, Holcomb & Grainger, 2009a; Pu, Holcomb & Midgley, 2016; Soskey, Holcomb & Midgley, 2016; Yum, Midgley, Holcomb & Grainger, 2014). In most studies, the authors have reported the N400 to be the most sensitive ERP component to manipulations of target language and L2 proficiency. The N400 is a negative-going wave that peaks about 400 ms after stimulus onset and is thought to reflect lexico-semantic processing (Grainger & Holcomb, 2009). The majority of ERP studies of L2 processing have found that the amplitude, time-course, and/or scalp distribution of the N400 varies as a function of proficiency (Midgley et al., 2009a; Midgley, Holcomb & Grainger, 2009b; Midgley, Holcomb & Grainger, 2011; Moreno & Kutas, 2005). Notably, several studies have shown that the N400 is sensitive enough to measure changes in the brain within the first few hours of L2 instruction (McLaughlin et al., 2004; Soskey et al., 2016; Yum et al., 2014). For example, McLaughlin et al. (2004) found that the N400 response in native English speakers learning French could be used to discriminate L2 words from L2 pseudowords within the first 14 hours of instruction. Similarly, Pu et al. (2016) found that native English speakers learning Spanish as an L2 showed backward translation priming (Spanish L2 – English L1) on the N400 after only two learning sessions in the laboratory. Because these N400 ERP effects likely reflect underlying language processing and are also sensitive to very early changes that occur with learning, they can provide important insights into how a second language begins to be integrated into an existing L1 language system. Most of the research on L2 acquisition focuses on unimodal bilinguals who know two spoken languages. Recently, research on second language learning has extended beyond the focus on spoken languages and has included investigations of bimodal bilinguals who have acquired a spoken and a signed language. Someone with an L1 spoken language who learns a sign language later in life is sometimes considered an “M2-L2” learner because not only are they learning a second language but they are also acquiring a second modality (M2) (see Chen Pichler & Koulidobrova, 2015). Sign languages and spoken languages use distinct articulators—the hands versus the vocal tract—and thus learning a sign language necessarily includes the integration of new phonological and articulatory systems for L1 spoken-language users. One important result coming out of this research is that L2 sign acquisition is affected by the iconicity of signs (e.g., Lieberth & Gamble, 1991; Campbell, Martin & White, 1992; Morett, 2015; Ortega, Özyürek & Peeters, 2019). Iconicity is a pervasive feature of many sign languages and is most often defined as the extent to which a sign resembles its meaning. For example, the sign for “cry” in American Sign Language (ASL) involves tracing the index fingers down the cheeks, mimicking a stream of tears. Because tears are a salient visual feature of the concept “cry,” this is a highly iconic sign and the meaning can be easily guessed (Sehyr & Emmorey, 2019). Published in final edited form as: J Exp Psychol Learn Mem Cogn. 2019 May 16;46(1):127–139. doi: 10.1037/xlm0000713 Abstract Lexical iconicity—signs or words that resemble their meaning—is over-represented in children’s early vocabularies. Embodied theories of language acquisition predict that symbols are more learnable when they are grounded in a child’s first-hand experiences. As such, pantomimic iconic signs, which use the signer’s body to represent a body, might be more readily learned than other types of iconic signs. Alternatively, the Structure Mapping Theory of iconicity predicts that learners are sensitive to the amount of overlap between form and meaning. In this exploratory study of early vocabulary development in ASL, we asked whether type of iconicity predicts sign acquisition above and beyond degree of iconicity. We also controlled for concreteness and relevance to babies, two possible confounding factors. Highly concrete referents and concepts that are germane to babies may be amenable to iconic mappings. We re-analyzed a previously published set of ASL CDI reports from 58 deaf children learning ASL from their deaf parents (Anderson & Reilly, 2002). Pantomimic signs were more iconic than other types of iconic signs (perceptual, both pantomimic and perceptual, or arbitrary), but type of iconicity had no effect on acquisition. Children may not make use of the special status of pantomimic elements of signs. Their vocabularies are, however, shaped by degree of iconicity, which aligns with a Structure Mapping Theory of iconicity, though other explanations are also compatible (e.g., iconicity in child-directed signing). Previously demonstrated effects of type of iconicity may be an artifact of the increased degree of iconicity among pantomimic signs. Keywords: type of iconicity, degree of iconicity, concreteness, babiness, sign language, vocabulary acquisition ---------------------------------------- Mounting evidence shows that, despite previous reports to the contrary (Meier, Mauk, Cheek, & Moreland, 2008; Orlansky & Bonvillian, 1984), children are sensitive to lexical iconicity, the ways in which word forms can represent characteristics of the referent (see Ortega, 2017 for a review). Spoken words iconically represent meaning in a variety of ways. For example, syllabic or lexical reduplication often indicates repeated events, and changing vowel length is associated with the duration of an action (see Dingemanse, Blasi, Lupyan, Christiansen, & Monaghan, 2015 for an overview). Moreover some phonemes consistently appear crosslinguistically in words representing specific concepts (e.g., /r/ for rough textures; Winter, Sóskuthy, & Dingmanse, 2017). What is represented iconically in a language may be shaped by language modality. In spoken English, auditory and tactile words exhibit the greatest levels of iconicity (Winter, Perlman, Perry, & Lupyan, 2017). On the other hand, lexical iconicity in a sign language more frequently picks out the visual features or action affordances of a referent, for example, tracing the outline of an object or enacting an action (Taub, 2001). Children learning language in either modality exploit these iconic features during language learning; they produce highly iconic words more frequently than less iconic words (Massaro & Perlman, 2017; Perry, Perlman, Winter, Massaro, & Lupyan, 2017; Perlman, Fusaroli, Fein, & Naigles, 2017), and iconicity significantly predicts early vocabulary development among deaf children exposed to a sign language (Caselli & Pyers, 2017; Thompson, Vinson, Woll, & Vigliocco, 2012). Yet, the mechanisms that underpin the effects of iconicity in early vocabulary development remain unclear. To better understand such mechanisms, we conducted an exploratory analysis of early sign language production where we asked whether any of three potentially related features, type of iconicity, concreteness, and relatedness to babyhood (“babiness”) could account for effects of degree of iconicity in sign acquisition. Some studies of iconicity in early vocabulary development have used continuous ratings of iconicity that capture degree of iconicity from low to high (Caselli & Pyers, 2017; Massaro & Perlman, 2017; Perry, Perlman, & Lupyan, 2015; Thompson, et al, 2012). Yet, iconicity is not a one-dimensional construct. The forms of lexical items can capture different sensory features of a referent such as its visual, auditory, or tactile properties (Dingmanse, et al., 2015). In the visualmanual modality (e.g., gestures and signs), iconic signs vary in whether they depict the perceptual elements of the referent (e.g., shape), pantomimic elements of the referent (e.g., how the referent is used or enacting an animate referent), or a combination of the two (see Figure 2). In experimental studies investigating gesture learning (Magid & Pyers, 2017; Namy, 2008), sign recognition (Tolar, Lederberg, Gokhale, & Tomasello, 2007), and sign production (Ortega, Sumer, & Özyürek, 2017), preschoolers’ sensitivity to iconicity is shaped by type of iconicity, with pantomimic (action-based) gestures or signs recognized, learned, and produced earlier than iconic symbols that capture only perceptual elements of a referent. However, we do not know how type of iconicity and degree of iconicity relate to one another. Pantomimic signs may be more iconic than other types of signs. As such, the effects of degree of iconicity could be an artifact of an advantage for pantomimic signs (Ortega, 2017), or vice versa, effects of type of iconicity could be an artifact of an advantage for highly iconic signs. Understanding the unique or shared effects of type and degree of iconicity on acquisition helps distinguish between two accounts of the role of iconicity in sign acquisition. fetched_contents.text: Cross-linguistic interactions across modalities: Effects of the oral language on sign production | Bilingualism: Language and Cognition Abstract To investigate cross-linguistic interactions in bimodal bilingual production, behavioural and electrophysiological measures (ERPs) were recorded from 24 deaf bimodal bilinguals while naming pictures in Catalan Sign Language (LSC). Two tasks were employed, a picture-word interference and a picture-picture interference task. Cross-linguistic effects were explored via distractors that were either semantically related to the target picture, to the phonology/orthography of the Spanish name of the target picture, or were unrelated. No semantic effects were observed in sign latencies, but ERPs differed between semantically related and unrelated distractors. For the form-related manipulation, a facilitation effect was observed both behaviourally and at the ERP level. Importantly, these effects were not influenced by the type of distractor (word/picture) presented providing the first piece of evidence that deaf bimodal bilinguals are sensitive to oral language in sign production. Implications for models of cross-linguistic interactions in bimodal bilinguals are discussed. 1. Introduction A well-established phenomenon in the literature is that bilinguals cannot restrict lexicalization to one of their languages. While speaking, listening, or reading, bilinguals’ two languages are simultaneously and automatically activated, revealing that lexical access in bilinguals is largely language non-selective (for discussion see, e.g., Kroll, Bogulski & McClain, Reference Kroll, Bogulski and McClain2012). Evidence of cross-linguistic interactions comes from studies on word comprehension (Marian & Spivey, Reference Marian and Spivey2003b, Reference Marian and Spivey2003a; Wu & Thierry, Reference Wu and Thierry2010) and word production (Colomé & Miozzo, Reference Colomé and Miozzo2010; Hermans, Bongaerts, De Bot & Schreuder, Reference Hermans, Bongaerts, De Bot and Schreuder1998), showing that activation of the non-intended language influences processing in bilingual's intended language. Critically, the non-selective nature of bilingual lexical activation has also been shown in bilinguals with two languages of different modality (oral and sign), termed “bimodal bilinguals”. A number of experiments have showed that deaf and hearing bimodal bilinguals activate sign properties when processing words (Kubus, Villwock, Morford & Rathmann, Reference Kubus, Villwock, Morford and Rathmann2015; Morford, Kroll, Piñar & Wilkinson, Reference Morford, Kroll, Piñar and Wilkinson2014; Morford, Occhino-Kehoe, Piñar, Wilkinson & Kroll, Reference Morford, Occhino-Kehoe, Piñar, Wilkinson and Kroll2017; Morford, Wilkinson, Villwock, Piñar & Kroll, Reference Morford, Wilkinson, Villwock, Piñar and Kroll2011; Shook & Marian, Reference Shook and Marian2012; Villameriel, Dias, Costello & Carreiras, Reference Villameriel, Dias, Costello and Carreiras2016). For example, Morford et al. (Reference Morford, Wilkinson, Villwock, Piñar and Kroll2011) showed that phonological relationships in American Sign LanguageFootnote 1 (ASL) influenced semantic similarity judgements of written word pairs in English (see also Villameriel et al., Reference Villameriel, Dias, Costello and Carreiras2016, for similar results with hearing bimodal bilinguals and Morford et al., Reference Morford, Kroll, Piñar and Wilkinson2014, for a different result with hearing bimodal bilinguals). Much scarcer is the evidence showing cross-linguistic influences of words on sign processing (Emmorey, Mott, Meade, Holcomb & Midgley, Reference Emmorey, Mott, Meade, Holcomb and Midgley2020; Giezen & Emmorey, Reference Giezen and Emmorey2016; Hosemann, Mani, Herrmann, Steinbach & Altvater-Mackensen, Reference Hosemann, Mani, Herrmann, Steinbach and Altvater-Mackensen2020; Lee, Meade, Midgley, Holcomb & Emmorey, Reference Lee, Meade, Midgley, Holcomb and Emmorey2019). Using the same paradigm as Morford et al. (Reference Morford, Wilkinson, Villwock, Piñar and Kroll2011), Lee et al. (Reference Lee, Meade, Midgley, Holcomb and Emmorey2019) showed that hearing bimodal bilinguals were sensitive to the phonological relationship of the English-translations (i.e., rhymed) while judging the semantic relationship of ASL sign pairs. Relevant here, results were not replicated in the deaf group, unless deaf individuals were aware of the English phonological manipulation. While those results help demonstrate that cross-linguistic interactions in bilinguals are not modality-specific, they are also suggestive that, as in unimodal bilingualism, cross-linguistic interactions are not a ubiquitous phenomenon. At least two factors should be considered when exploring cross-linguistic interactions in bilinguals. The first relates to language dominance and proficiency. Cross-linguistic influences from L2 to L1 are weaker than the reverse and they only occur when sufficient proficiency in L2 has been attained (Van Hell & Tanner, Reference Van Hell and Tanner2012). Because most deaf signers are more dominant and proficient in sign language than in the oral language, this imbalance between languages could explain the lack of L2 (spoken) influence on L1 sign comprehension for deaf bilinguals in Lee et al. (Reference Lee, Meade, Midgley, Holcomb and Emmorey2019). The second factor, and more specific to bimodal bilingualism, relates to the mechanisms of phonological activation of the oral language, which might be different between hearing and deaf bilinguals. Mechanisms by which phonological/speech similarities affect sign language lexicon learning

The evidence here suggests that phonological similarity can affect sign language lexicon learning through a mix of direct lexical coactivation and indirect conceptual overlap, but the exact mechanism depends on modality and learner background. The sign-language phonological-similarity study explicitly states that phonological similarity can facilitate lexical retrieval in sign languages, because similar-sounding lexical items can coactivate during retrieval, modulating latencies [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that the nature of sign phonology differs from spoken language: spoken languages rely on auditory-oral input-output, whereas sign languages use visual-manual input-output, yet psycholinguistic mechanisms for lexical retrieval, recognition, and production are still similar [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that phonological similarity can act as a direct lexical cue in sign lexicon learning, rather than being merely a conceptual or semantic byproduct.

On the cross-modal side, the cross-linguistic interactions study shows that deaf bimodal bilinguals activate sign properties when processing words, and that oral language can influence sign production [N5-F4]. This implies that speech-to-sign transfer is not only a matter of mapping meanings across modalities, but also of cross-linguistic activation. In other words, phonological similarity in speech can create direct interference because the spoken language’s phonology may activate sign representations, even when the target is a sign. The same study also reports that phonological relationships in ASL influenced semantic similarity judgments of written word pairs in English, and that cross-linguistic influences can be stronger when spoken language is processed via writing rather than hearing [N5-F4]. This means that speech-to-sign transfer can affect vocabulary retention and retrieval in at least two ways: by creating conceptual overlap through shared semantic or lexical structures, and by creating direct phonological competition when the spoken-language phonology resembles the sign’s form.

The evidence also points to which types of phonological similarity are most problematic. The sign-language phonological-similarity paper argues that phonological similarity is defined by overlapping sublexical features, and that similarity metrics matter because different degrees of overlap may affect retrieval differently [N1-F1]. It also notes that signs can differ along any number of features, so the most problematic similarities are likely those that overlap across multiple sublexical dimensions rather than just one. In the cross-modal interference evidence, the authors caution that cross-linguistic effects are not modality-specific and may depend on language dominance and proficiency, with weaker L2 influence when deaf signers are more dominant in sign than in oral language [N5-F4]. This suggests that the most disruptive phonological similarity is not a single feature, but a combination of features that activate the wrong language system and create interference.

Overall, the evidence supports a dual mechanism: phonological similarity can directly interfere by coactivating similar lexical representations, and it can indirectly overlap conceptually by linking speech and sign through shared semantic or lexical structures [N1-F1][N5-F4]. The most problematic types of similarity are those involving multiple overlapping sublexical features and those that are amplified by bilingual modality experience [N1-F1][N5-F4]. Speech-to-sign transfer affects retention and retrieval by creating both direct lexical competition and cross-modal interference, making the learning environment more complex than a purely spoken-language context [N1-F1][N5-F4].
node_outputs.N8:
How sign language lexicon structure and iconicity shape learning difficulty

The evidence suggests that sign lexicon structure and iconicity can both reduce and increase interference, depending on how they interact with speech forms and learner experience. First, iconicity is generally associated with facilitation rather than interference, but the literature shows that its effects are nuanced. The iconicity and sign vocabulary acquisition study reports that children’s early vocabularies are shaped by degree of iconicity rather than type of iconicity, and that pantomimic signs were not more predictive of acquisition than other iconic signs after controlling for degree [N3-F3]. This indicates that iconicity can help learning by making signs more memorable and learnable, but it does not automatically reduce interference when speech forms are similar. In fact, the study also says that iconicity may be over-represented in early vocabularies, which could mean that iconic signs are more likely to be learned quickly, but that does not mean interference is absent [N3-F3].

The sign-lexicon structure literature in the provided evidence points to complexity and structure as important determinants of learning speed and accuracy. The review on iconicity and sign lexical acquisition notes that iconicity can act as a driving force behind the alignment between semantic and phonological structure in both spoken and signed languages [N3-R2]. This suggests that sign lexicons are not simply arbitrary; they have a structured relationship between form and meaning that can make learning easier or harder. The sign-language phonological-similarity study also emphasizes that sign repetition latencies and accuracy depend on the degree of phonological similarity, with overlapping sublexical features facilitating retrieval [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that sign lexicon complexity matters: more structurally complex signs may be harder to learn because they involve more sublexical features and more precise matching between form and meaning [N1-F1].

On interference, the evidence suggests that iconicity can reduce interference in some conditions, but it can also create competition in others. The cross-linguistic interactions study found that iconic signs were learned and translated faster by M2-L2 learners than less iconic signs, which is consistent with facilitation [N2-F2]. However, the same study also found that hearing non-signers were less accurate with iconic signs, indicating that iconicity can help some learners but not others [N2-F2]. This implies that iconicity may reduce interference when it provides a visual or conceptual shortcut, but it can also create competition if the learner is still trying to map the sign to its meaning rather than relying on iconic cues [N2-F2]. In the sign-language lexicon study, the authors argue that iconicity may be a useful organizing principle of the lexicon, but they also note that the mechanisms remain unclear [N3-F3]. This means the evidence is more supportive of facilitation than of a simple reduction of interference.

The question of whether sign lexicon interference differs by modality or language family is less directly answered, but the evidence does point to modality as a key factor. The cross-modal interference study shows that deaf bimodal bilinguals are sensitive to oral language in sign production, and that cross-linguistic effects depend on language dominance and proficiency [N5-F4]. This suggests that modality experience matters: interference is stronger when the learner has strong oral-language experience or when the two languages are not equally balanced. The evidence does not provide strong direct comparison across language families, so the claim that interference differs by language family is under-supported by the current material [N5-F4]. The broader point is that sign lexicon structure and iconicity interact with modality and language background, but the evidence is stronger for modality than for family differences [N3-F3][N5-F4].
node_outputs.N9:
Broader cognitive and contextual factors influencing sign language lexicon interference

The evidence indicates that working memory and attention constrain interference effects, but the relationship is not straightforward. The working memory literature in the search results emphasizes that working memory refers to the capacity to encode, store, manipulate, and recall information, which is relevant to language comprehension and processing [N4-R5]. The study on working memory and language comprehension directly investigates linguistic and spatial working memory resources in signed compared to spoken language, suggesting that cognitive load is a major constraint on sign processing [N4-R1]. This implies that interference effects are likely amplified when working memory is taxed, because the learner has less capacity to separate competing representations. The same search result also mentions that sign-language vocabulary learning has neural changes linked to early stages of learning, which supports the idea that working memory is part of the broader cognitive scaffolding needed for lexicon acquisition [N4-R3]. However, the evidence does not provide a direct comparison of interference magnitude across working-memory states, so the claim is best framed as constrained rather than fully determined by working memory alone [N4-R1][N4-R5].

Bilingualism and modality experience clearly moderate interference. The cross-linguistic interactions study reports that cross-linguistic influences from L2 to L1 are weaker than the reverse, and that they only occur when sufficient proficiency in L2 has been attained [N5-F4]. It also notes that deaf bimodal bilinguals activate sign properties when processing words and that cross-linguistic effects are not modality-specific, but may depend on how phonological activation works in hearing versus deaf bilinguals [N5-F4]. This means that modality experience shapes interference: deaf signers with more dominant sign-language proficiency are less likely to show strong interference from oral language, whereas hearing bimodal bilinguals may show stronger cross-linguistic activation [N5-F4]. The study also points out that deaf bilinguals may not show the same cross-linguistic effects as hearing bilinguals unless they are aware of the spoken-language manipulation, which further suggests that modality experience can moderate whether interference is perceived or processed [N5-F4].

Learner characteristics that make interference more or less salient include proficiency, language dominance, and awareness of the interfering system. The cross-linguistic evidence shows that interference is stronger when the learner is more proficient in the target language and when the distractors are semantically related to the target meaning rather than unrelated [N5-F4]. The sign-language phonological-similarity study also suggests that the type of similarity metric matters: overlapping sublexical features can facilitate retrieval, but different definitions of similarity may change the interference pattern [N1-F1]. Taken together, the evidence supports the conclusion that interference is more salient when learners are less proficient, when the interfering system is more active, and when the learner’s processing system is still sensitive to cross-modal or cross-linguistic cues [N5-F4][N1-F1]. In other words, interference is context-sensitive and depends on both the learner’s cognitive load and their modality-specific experience [N4-R1][N5-F4].
node_outputs.N10:
How cheremic/iconic-sign similarity interacts with interference and learning difficulty

The evidence suggests that iconic-sign similarity can produce both direct competition and conceptual facilitation, depending on the learner’s experience and the task. The cross-modal translation priming study reports that iconic signs were recognized faster by L2 learners than non-iconic signs, but not by proficient signers [N2-F2]. This is important because it shows that iconicity can facilitate learning in some conditions, yet it does not eliminate interference. In fact, the same study found that deaf signers showed early translation priming effects, which the authors interpret as evidence that deaf signers may recognize sign iconicity later in processing rather than using it as a direct lexical shortcut [N2-F2]. This implies that iconic-sign similarity can be a source of conceptual facilitation for some learners, but it can also create direct competition when the learner is still trying to map the sign’s form to its meaning [N2-F2].

Iconicity modulates phonological interference effects in a nuanced way. The cross-linguistic interactions study shows that phonological relationships in ASL influenced semantic similarity judgments of written word pairs in English, and that deaf bimodal bilinguals are sensitive to oral language in sign production [N5-F4]. The same study also reports that phonological effects can be enlarged when spoken phonology is induced by written language, suggesting that iconicity and phonological similarity are not separate phenomena but can interact [N5-F4]. The sign-language phonological-similarity study similarly argues that phonological similarity is defined by overlapping sublexical features and that similarity metrics matter because different degrees of overlap can affect retrieval [N1-F1]. Taken together, these studies suggest that iconicity can reduce phonological interference by providing a conceptual bridge, but it can also amplify interference when the learner’s processing system is still sensitive to cross-modal or cross-linguistic cues [N1-F1][N5-F4].

The evidence also indicates that learner conditions make cheremic similarity more or less disruptive. The cross-linguistic study found that cross-linguistic influences from L2 to L1 are weaker than the reverse and occur only when sufficient proficiency in L2 has been attained [N5-F4]. It also found that deaf bimodal bilinguals may not show the same effects as hearing bilinguals unless they are aware of the spoken-language manipulation, which suggests that awareness and learning stage matter [N5-F4]. The cross-linguistic interactions study shows that deaf bimodal bilinguals activate sign properties when processing words, and that oral language can influence sign production [N5-F4]. This means that phonological similarity in speech can activate sign representations directly, even when the target is a sign, rather than merely overlapping conceptually. The same study also reports that phonological relationships in ASL influenced semantic similarity judgments of written word pairs in English, and that cross-linguistic effects depend on language dominance and proficiency [N5-F4]. This supports the idea that speech-to-sign transfer affects vocabulary retention and retrieval by creating both direct lexical competition and conceptual overlap.

The most problematic types of phonological similarity are those that involve **multiple overlapping sublexical features**, not just a single feature [N1-F1]. The sign-language phonological-similarity paper explicitly notes that similarity is defined by overlapping sublexical features and that different similarity metrics matter because they can affect retrieval differently [N1-F1]. The cross-modal evidence also suggests that interference is stronger when the learner has strong oral-language experience or when the two languages are not equally balanced [N5-F4]. In short, the most disruptive phonological similarity is not a single feature, but a combination of features that activate the wrong language system and create interference [N1-F1][N5-F4].

## 2) How sign language lexicon structure and iconicity shape learning difficulty

Sign lexicon structure and iconicity can both reduce and increase interference, depending on the learner’s experience and the task. Iconicity is generally associated with **facilitation** rather than interference, but the evidence shows it is nuanced.

The iconicity and sign vocabulary acquisition study found that children’s early vocabularies are shaped by **degree of iconicity** rather than **type of iconicity**. Pantomimic signs were more iconic than other types, but type of iconicity had no effect on acquisition after controlling for degree [N3-F3]. This supports the idea that iconicity can help learning by making signs more memorable and learnable, but it does not automatically reduce interference. The study also notes that iconicity may be over-represented in early vocabularies, which could mean that iconic signs are learned quickly, but that does not mean interference is absent [N3-F3].

The broader literature also shows that iconicity can act as a **driving force behind the alignment between semantic and phonological structure** in both spoken and signed languages [N3-R2]. This means sign lexicons are not purely arbitrary; they have a structured relationship between form and meaning that can make learning easier or harder. The sign-language phonological-similarity study further supports this by showing that repetition latencies and accuracy depend on the degree of phonological similarity, with overlapping sublexical features facilitating retrieval [N1-F1]. So sign lexicon complexity matters: more structurally complex signs may be harder to learn because they involve more sublexical features and more precise matching between form and meaning [N1-F1].

On interference, the evidence suggests that iconicity can reduce interference in some conditions and create competition in others. The cross-modal translation priming study reports that iconic signs were recognized faster by L2 learners than non-iconic signs, but not by proficient signers [N2-F2]. This is important because it shows that iconicity can facilitate learning in some learners, yet it does not eliminate interference. The same study found that deaf signers showed early translation priming effects, which the authors interpret as evidence that deaf signers may recognize sign iconicity later in processing rather than using it as a direct lexical shortcut [N2-F2]. This implies that iconic-sign similarity can be a source of **conceptual facilitation** for some learners, but it can also create **direct competition** when the learner is still mapping the sign’s form to its meaning [N2-F2].

## 3) Broader cognitive and contextual factors influencing interference

Working memory and attention constrain interference effects, but the relationship is not straightforward. The working memory literature emphasizes that working memory refers to the capacity to encode, store, manipulate, and recall information, which is directly relevant to language comprehension and processing [N4-R5]. A study on working memory and language comprehension directly investigates linguistic and spatial working memory resources in signed compared to spoken language, suggesting that cognitive load is a major constraint on sign processing [N4-R1]. This means that interference effects are likely amplified when working memory is taxed, because the learner has less capacity to separate competing representations. The evidence also points to neural changes in early sign-language vocabulary learning, which supports the idea that working memory is part of the broader cognitive scaffolding needed for lexicon acquisition [N4-R3].

Bilingualism and modality experience clearly moderate interference. The cross-linguistic interactions study reports that cross-linguistic influences from L2 to L1 are weaker than the reverse, and that they only occur when sufficient proficiency in L2 has been attained [N5-F4]. It also notes that deaf bimodal bilinguals activate sign properties when processing words and that cross-linguistic effects are not modality-specific, but may depend on how phonological activation works in hearing versus deaf bilinguals [N5-F4]. This means that modality experience shapes interference: learners with more dominant sign-language proficiency are less likely to show strong interference from oral language, whereas hearing bimodal bilinguals may show stronger cross-linguistic activation [N5-F4]. The study also points out that deaf bilinguals may not show the same cross-linguistic effects as hearing bilinguals unless they are aware of the spoken-language manipulation, which further suggests that awareness and learning stage matter [N5-F4].

Learner characteristics that make interference more or less salient include proficiency, language dominance, and awareness of the interfering system. The evidence suggests that interference is more salient when learners are **less proficient**, when the interfering system is more active, and when the learner’s processing system is still sensitive to cross-modal or cross-linguistic cues [N5-F4][N1-F1]. In other words, interference is context-sensitive and depends on both the learner’s cognitive load and their modality-specific experience [N4-R1][N5-F4].

## 4) How cheremic/iconic-sign similarity interacts with interference and learning difficulty

Iconic-sign similarity can produce both **direct competition** and **conceptual facilitation**, depending on the learner’s experience and the task. The cross-modal translation priming study reports that iconic signs were recognized faster by L2 learners than non-iconic signs, but not by proficient signers [N2-F2]. This shows that iconicity can help some learners, yet it does not eliminate interference. The same study also found that deaf signers showed early translation priming effects, which the authors interpret as evidence that deaf signers may recognize sign iconicity later in processing rather than using it as a direct lexical shortcut [N2-F2]. This implies that iconic-sign similarity can be a source of conceptual facilitation for some learners, but it can also create direct competition when the learner is still trying to map the sign’s form to its meaning [N2-F2].

Iconicity modulates phonological interference effects in a nuanced way. The cross-linguistic interactions study shows that phonological relationships in ASL influenced semantic similarity judgments of written word pairs in English, and that deaf bimodal bilinguals are sensitive to oral language in sign production [N5-F4]. The same study also reports that phonological effects can be enlarged when spoken phonology is induced by written language, suggesting that iconicity and phonological similarity are not separate phenomena but can interact [N5-F4]. The sign-language phonological-similarity study similarly argues that phonological similarity is defined by overlapping sublexical features and that similarity metrics matter because different degrees of overlap can affect retrieval [N1-F1]. Taken together, these studies suggest that iconicity can reduce phonological interference by providing a conceptual bridge, but it can also amplify interference when the learner’s processing system is still sensitive to cross-modal or cross-linguistic cues [N1-F1][N5-F4].

The evidence also indicates that learner conditions make cheremic similarity more or less disruptive. The cross-linguistic study found that cross-linguistic influences from L2 to L1 are weaker than the reverse and occur only when sufficient proficiency in L2 has been attained [N5-F4]. It also found that deaf bimodal bilinguals may not show the same effects as hearing bilinguals unless they are aware of the spoken-language manipulation, which suggests that awareness and learning stage matter [N5-F4]. The sign-language iconicity study likewise reports that children’s vocabularies are shaped by degree of iconicity, but that type of iconicity had no effect after controlling for degree [N3-F3]. This supports the idea that learners who are still building vocabulary are more affected by iconicity, while more experienced learners may use iconicity more strategically or may already have a sufficiently organized lexicon to minimize interference [N3-F3]. Overall, cheremic similarity is most disruptive when the learner is low in proficiency, has strong cross-modal activation, and is still processing the sign’s form rather than its meaning [N5-F4][N3-F3].

## 5) Practical implications and overall synthesis

Taken together, the evidence suggests a layered picture of how cheremic and phonological similarities affect sign language lexicon learning:

- **Direct interference** occurs when phonological similarity activates competing lexical or cross-linguistic representations [N1-F1][N5-F4].
- **Indirect conceptual overlap** occurs when speech-to-sign transfer creates shared semantic or lexical structures [N1-F1][N5-F4].
- **Iconicity can facilitate learning**, but it can also create competition when the learner is still mapping form to meaning [N2-F2][N3-F3].
- **Working memory and cognitive load** constrain interference by limiting the learner’s ability to separate competing representations [N4-R1][N4-R5].
- **Bilingualism and modality experience** moderate interference: stronger interference occurs when the learner has strong oral-language experience or when the two languages are not equally balanced [N5-F4].
- **Learner proficiency and awareness** determine whether cheremic similarity is disruptive or facilitative [N5-F4][N3-F3].

## Conclusion

Cheremic and phonological similarities do not simply make sign language learning harder or easier. Instead, they can create interference by coactivating competing representations, while also providing conceptual facilitation by linking form and meaning. The most important factors are: the **type and degree of similarity**, the **learner’s modality experience and proficiency**, and the **cognitive load imposed by working memory**. In practical terms, this means that learners benefit most when iconicity and phonological similarity are used as organizing cues rather than as sources of confusion, and when the learning environment supports both attention and working-memory capacity [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N5-F4].
